blocks.text: Pharmacodynamics is the study of the mechanism of action of drugs (the effect of drugs on the body). Most psychotropics affect brain neurotransmitters, and this can occur at various levels of the neurotransmission cycle.

blocks.title: Level of action in the neurotransmission cycle
rows: Benzodiazepines at **GABA-A** complex; bromocriptine for dopamine

blocks.forTopic: Levels of action in the neurotransmission cycle

blocks.text: The notes direct the reader to the Neurochemistry **SPMM** notes for more detail on the different neurotransmitters, their structure and receptor actions.

blocks.subtopic: Enzymes that degrade dopamine and MAO substrates
blocks.note: The notes list **MAO** inhibitors as acting at degradation but do not state which enzymes metabolise dopamine or the **MAO-A**/**MAO-B** substrates. **Q7** answers **MAO-B** and **COMT** for most body dopamine; its explanation says **MAO-A** preferentially deaminates serotonin and norepinephrine and **MAO-B** deaminates dopamine, histamine and phenylethylamines. **Q9** (answer: epinephrine, dopamine and serotonin) rests on the same explanation.

blocks.text: **MAO** substrates are keyed as epinephrine, dopamine and serotonin, and the distractors pair these with acetylcholine, tyramine or histamine; the explanation says **MAO-A** preferentially deaminates serotonin and norepinephrine while **MAO-B** deaminates dopamine, histamine and phenylethylamines. Do not confuse this with the enzyme question (most body dopamine is metabolised by **MAO-B** and **COMT**, not **MAO-A**).

bullets.text: Pharmacodynamics = mechanism of action of drugs (effect of drugs on the body).
Psychotropics act at different levels: synthesis, storage, release, reuptake, degradation, pre/postsynaptic receptors, second messengers.
Reserpine depletes NA and DA stores; amphetamine stimulates NA and DA release.
Reuptake: SSRI, TCA, cocaine; bupropion blocks dopamine and noradrenaline reuptake.
Degradation: MAO inhibitors and acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (e.g. donepezil).
Partial agonists: aripiprazole (D2), buspirone (5HT1A), clonazepam (BDZ receptor), buprenorphine (mu). Lithium acts at the inositol second messenger level.
MAO substrates: epinephrine, dopamine, serotonin (MAO-A: serotonin, norepinephrine; MAO-B: dopamine, histamine).

blocks.text: A drug receptor is the cellular component to which the drug binds and through which it initiates its pharmacodynamic effects. There are 2 major superfamilies: ionotropic and metabotropic receptors.

blocks.title: Ionotropic vs metabotropic receptors
rows: Act through G-proteins that bind the intracellular portion of the receptor and activate a second messenger
Rapid transient increase in membrane permeability to cations (sodium, calcium) or anions (chloride); excitation or inhibition of the postsynaptic membrane
Slower response; altered second messenger levels change the phosphorylation state of key proteins, making them active or inactive
Dopamine (**D1-5**), noradrenaline, serotonin 5HT1-7 except 5HT3, muscarinic acetylcholine, opioid (mu)

blocks.text: 'All nicotinic receptors are excitatory' is the true statement: nicotinic acetylcholine receptors are excitatory ligand-gated ion channels in the same superfamily as **GABA-A**. The explanation attributes the anticholinergic effects of psychotropics and fine motor disturbances to the **MUSCARINIC** group, not nicotinic, and says blocking nicotinic receptors gives gross neuromuscular paralysis.

For glutamate the keyed true statement is that it acts via **NMDA** receptors; the distractors (inhibitory transmitter, all receptors ionotropic, chloride channels, synthesised by glutamate decarboxylase) are wrong, and the explanation stresses that glutamate decarboxylase (**GAD**) converts glutamate to **GABA**, so **GABA**, not glutamate, is the product of **GAD**.
A drug can be an agonist, which stimulates the biological activity of a receptor, or an antagonist, which inhibits it.

Full agonists produce a maximal response, measured against physiological neurotransmitter efficiency for the receptor. Partial agonists cannot elicit a maximal response and are less effective than full agonists (examples: **aripiprazole**, **buspirone**, **buprenorphine**); they have a ceiling effect.

The response to a partial agonist depends on availability of physiological neurotransmitter: when maximal dopamine is available, **aripiprazole** can inhibit dopaminergic transmission because a less efficient molecule competes with a more efficient one; in dopamine-deficient states the same partial agonist can enhance dopaminergic effects.

The partial **D2** agonist is **aripiprazole**, not **risperidone**, **amisulpride**, **pramipexole** or **buspirone**; the explanation adds that it is also a 5-**HT1A** partial agonist, a high-affinity 5-**HT2A** antagonist, a low/moderate-affinity **H1** and alpha-1 antagonist and has no anticholinergic effect. The mirror question (**Q17**) keys **buspirone** as the 5HT1A partial agonist, with **aripiprazole** listed as a distractor.

**Aripiprazole** is **ANTAGONISTIC** at 5-**HT2A** receptors (the keyed answer); its actions at **D2** and 5-**HT1A** are **PARTIAL** **AGONISM**, not antagonism. The explanation lists minor actions as **H1**, alpha-1 and alpha-2 antagonism and diffuse muscarinic (**M1-M5**) antagonism.

An inverse agonist binds the same receptor but produces the opposite pharmacological effect. No clinical drug acts via this mechanism, but several have been researched, especially at the **GABA** complex. Antagonists interfere with receptor activation by neurotransmitter or other agonists.

blocks.title: Types of antagonism
rows: Can be reversed completely by increasing the agonist dose; reduces potency (minimal dose needed for an effect) but not efficacy (maximal response)
Atropine at muscarinic receptors; **propranolol** at beta-adrenergic receptors
Alters the receptor site, so increasing the agonist dose reverses the effect only partially; reduces both potency and efficacy (shifts the curve right and reduces the maximum effect)
Bind irreversibly to the target site
Opposing action of two molecules acting via the same receptors
Opposing action of two molecules acting via different receptors
Opposing action of two molecules via chemical reactions; not seen in psychotropics

blocks.mnemonic: Cats Never Ignore Pretty Pink Chairs

blocks.text: Most drugs bind reversibly and the response is proportional to the fraction of receptors occupied (law of mass action); as concentration rises the response rises until all receptors are occupied, giving a dose-response curve.

With therapeutic use, agonists may cause down-regulation (desensitivity: reduced receptor numbers) while antagonists may have the opposite effect, up-regulation (hypersensitivity: increased receptor numbers).

blocks.title: Potency, affinity and efficacy
rows: Amount of drug needed to produce a particular effect compared with a standard drug with a similar receptor profile. Determined by: (a) proportion of drug reaching the receptor, (b) affinity for the receptor, (c) efficacy
Ability of the drug to bind its appropriate receptor; the higher the affinity and the more receptors occupied, the more potent the drug generally is
How well the drug produces the expected response, i.e. the maximum clinical response; depends on affinity, potency, duration of receptor action in some cases and kinetic properties such as half-life

blocks.forTopic: Potency, affinity and efficacy (notes' one-word glosses)

blocks.text: **Haloperidol** is more potent than **chlorpromazine**: about 5 mg of **haloperidol** achieves the same effect as 100 mg of **chlorpromazine**. They are comparable in maximal clinical response, i.e. equally efficacious but not equipotent.

A drug-receptor complex's 'intrinsic activity' means **EFFICACY** of the resulting functional response (the capability to produce the highest functional response), not potency, affinity or the efficiency of a drug in reaching the receptor.

**Q27** describes drug X giving improvement at 10 mg and drug Y giving the same improvement at 20 mg; the correct answer is that X and Y are equally efficacious (same maximal response), the explanation defining efficacy as how well the drug produces the expected response. The dose difference is a potency difference, not an efficacy one.

**Q46** gives a non-competitive **NMDA** antagonist (drug A) and asks what happens if glutamate availability is raised: the effect of drug A is only partially reversed, because noncompetitive antagonism reduces both potency and efficacy of agonists. Do not choose full reversal (that is competitive antagonism).

blocks.note: **Q24** (answer: agonists) explanation states that an agonist binds a specific receptor producing an effect identical to the neurotransmitter, and drugs are often designed as agonists when the original neurotransmitter is missing or diminished. The notes define agonists only as stimulating receptor activity.

Not in the notes. Mock stem (keyed answer **AMPA**): the explanation says d-serine is an endogenous ligand for the glycine site of the **NMDA** receptor, and that some recent studies suggest a low-affinity, stereo-selective site at the agonist-binding pocket of **AMPA** receptors for D-amino acids such as d-serine.

bullets.text: Two receptor superfamilies: ionotropic (ligand-gated channels, quick) and metabotropic (G-protein, slower).
Ionotropic examples: nicotinic ACh, GABA-A, glutamate, 5HT3. Metabotropic: D1-5, noradrenaline, 5HT1-7 except 5HT3, muscarinic, mu opioid.
Partial agonist: submaximal response, ceiling effect; acts as inhibitor when full neurotransmitter is plentiful and as enhancer in deficiency (aripiprazole).
Inverse agonist: opposite effect; no clinical drug uses it.
Competitive antagonism: reversed fully by more agonist; lowers potency, not efficacy. Non-competitive: only partial reversal; lowers potency and efficacy.
Chronic agonist use may down-regulate receptors; antagonists may up-regulate them.
Haloperidol 5 mg = chlorpromazine 100 mg: more potent but equally efficacious.
Partial D2 agonist = aripiprazole (also 5-HT1A partial agonist, 5-HT2A antagonist).
Intrinsic activity = efficacy of the functional response.

sections.title: 3. Modes of therapeutic action for psychotropics: antipsychotic drugs

blocks.text: In general all antipsychotics act via varying degrees of **D2** blockade. Atypical drugs show selectivity for **D2** receptors and a high 5HT2:**D2** blocking ratio.

blocks.title: Antipsychotic mechanisms by drug
rows: **D2** and **D3** antagonism; dose-dependent pre- and postsynaptic profile similar to **sulpiride**; some limbic selectivity; 5HT7 activity also noted

Partial dopamine agonist at **D2**; also 5HT2A antagonist. 'Goldilocks' stabilising action: antagonises **DA** where it is excessive (mesolimbic) and mimics **DA** at deficient sites (mesocortical, linked to negative symptoms); little change in tuberoinfundibulum. Acts on postsynaptic **D2** receptors and presynaptic autoreceptors
**D2** antagonist and 5HT2A blocker (similar to **olanzapine**); potent alpha-2 blockade; sublingual; allegedly weight and prolactin-neutral; licensed for mania
Moderate antimuscarinic effect in addition to **D2** blockade; highly sedative phenothiazines

High 5HT2 to **D2** blockade ratio; also blocks **D4** and 5HT6; notable alpha 1 antagonism, anticholinergic and antihistaminic properties; weak **D1** and **D2** affinity; also binds 5HT3; proposed faster dissociation rate (like **quetiapine**), a 'hit and run' profile

**D2** antagonist and 5HT2A blocker (similar to **risperidone**); high affinity for 5HT7; partial agonist at 5HT1A; minimal affinity for alpha-1 (less orthostatic effect) and histamine receptors (thus may be weight neutral)
Atypical; high 5HT2/**D2** blockade ratio; potent **D4** and 5HT6 blockade; significant anticholinergic and some antihistaminic effects
Similar to **clozapine** - hit and run profile on **D2**; somewhat lesser 5HT2A blockade than other atypicals; significant anticholinergic effects similar to **olanzapine**
Serotonin-dopamine antagonist; high 5HT2A antagonism; at higher therapeutic doses binds **D2** like typicals, leading to extrapyramidal and prolactin-related side effects
Pure **D2** antagonist; at low doses presynaptic receptors blocked (helps negative symptoms?); above 800 mg/day affects postsynaptic **D2**, reducing positive symptoms
**D2** antagonists; marked antimuscarinic effect; fewer EPSEs than other typicals

Atypical with 5HT2A and **D2** blockade; antagonises 5HT1D, 5HT2C, **D3**, **D4**; poor muscarinic affinity; some antihistaminic property; agonistic at 5HT1A; some serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibition
Atypical with 5HT2A, 5HT2C, **D1**, **D2**, **D3**, **D4** antagonism; potent noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor; potent antihistaminic activity; some **NMDA** antagonism

blocks.title: Receptor-profile statements: notes vs question bank
rows: Hit and run profile on **D2**; somewhat lesser 5HT2A blockade than other atypicals
**Q32** explanation: some argue **quetiapine** has low **D2**/low 5HT2 activity
High 5HT2 to **D2** blockade ratio; weak **D1** and **D2** affinity
**Risperidone** has high 5HT2A antagonism and binds **D2** like typicals at higher doses
**Q32** (answer **risperidone**): **haloperidol** is high **D2**/low 5HT2; high **D2**/high 5HT2 is characteristic of **olanzapine**, **risperidone** and loxapine
**Q47** (answer **sulpiride**): **sulpiride** is a predominant **D2** antagonist with minimal **D3** antagonist/partial agonist actions; **amisulpride** is **D2**/**D3**

blocks.text: Therapeutic action of conventional antipsychotics = **D2** blockade in the **MESOLIMBIC** pathway; every other **D2** option is a side-effect pathway. The explanation: mesocortical blockade produces or worsens negative symptoms, nigrostriatal blockade causes EPSEs, tuberoinfundibular blockade causes hyperprolactinaemia features (galactorrhoea, sexual dysfunction, gynaecomastia, infertility, amenorrhoea, possibly osteoporosis); alpha-1 blockade causes sedation, dizziness and orthostatic hypotension.

blocks.forTopic: D2 pathways and the effect of blocking each

blocks.text: Raised prolactin follows blockade of the **TUBEROINFUNDIBULAR** pathway (hypothalamus to anterior pituitary), whose neurons are tonically active and inhibit prolactin release; mesolimbic blockade is the therapeutic one, not the prolactin one.

Amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea and loss of sexual desire on **amisulpride** are hyperprolactinaemia, due to **D2** blockade (and/or 5HT1A **STIMULATION**); 5HT1A antagonism, **D1**, **D3** and 5HT2A antagonism are the distractors. Dopamine inhibits prolactin release, so dopamine antagonists raise it.

High **D2**/high 5HT2 activity is **risperidone** (also **olanzapine** and loxapine); the distractors are **haloperidol** (high **D2**/**LOW** 5HT2), **clozapine** (**LOW** **D2**/high 5HT2) and **quetiapine** (argued low **D2**/low 5HT2).

**Sulpiride** is the predominant **D2** antagonist (minimal **D3** action), while **amisulpride** is a **D2**/**D3** antagonist: low-dose **amisulpride** blocks autoreceptors (raising synaptic dopamine, a possible reason for effects on negative symptoms) and in limbic regions blocks postsynaptic **D2**/**D3** to reduce positive symptoms.

Fastest to dissociate from the **D2** receptor is **clozapine** (not **aripiprazole**, xanomeline, **paliperidone** or **risperidone**): the explanation says fast dissociation, not high 5-**HT2** or **D4** affinity, is the single most powerful predictor of atypicality, and that **quetiapine** also binds loosely and dissociates quickly.

Akathisia on antipsychotics is attributed to **HIGH** **D2** receptor occupancy in the striatum (not low occupancy, receptor supersensitivity, hippocampal **D2** activation or 5-**HT2** blockade); higher doses correlate with higher **D2** occupancy and worse subjective akathisia, and most EPSEs track **D2** occupancy.

blocks.note: Not in the notes. Mock stem (keyed **D2** blockade): **D2** blockade by **chlorpromazine** in the chemoreceptor trigger zone explains its antiemetic property.

Not in the notes. Mock stem (keyed **M1**/**M4** agonism): xanomeline has been advocated as a novel approach for schizophrenia and acts via **M1**/**M4** agonism (stated as in Phase 3 trials in the explanation).

Not in the notes. Mock stem (keyed **aripiprazole**): adding **aripiprazole** to **clozapine** may be particularly effective in reversing metabolic effects such as weight gain and can be used as an augmenting agent.

items.text: **Amisulpride** is the atypical option among **fluphenazine**, promazine, **chlorpromazine**, amoxapine and **amisulpride**: selective, equipotent **D2**/**D3** antagonism, negligible affinity for other receptors, EPSEs like placebo at low doses but dose-dependent EPSEs and prolactinaemia at higher doses.
**Buspirone** is the 5HT1A partial agonist (**pramipexole**, **amisulpride**, **risperidone** and **aripiprazole** are the distractors); **aripiprazole** is the **D2** partial agonist (**Q28**).

Hyperprolactinaemia after **risperidone** plus **lofepramine** is blamed on the neuroleptic: dopamine blockade causes breast enlargement and galactorrhoea in women and suppresses testosterone in men; **haloperidol** and **chlorpromazine** are particularly prone.
**Chlorpromazine**'s antiemetic property = **D2** blockade in the chemoreceptor trigger zone.

bullets.text: All antipsychotics act via varying degrees of D2 blockade; atypicals have a high 5HT2:D2 blocking ratio.
Aripiprazole: partial D2 agonist plus 5HT2A antagonist; Goldilocks stabilising action (antagonist in mesolimbic, agonist in mesocortical).
Clozapine and quetiapine: faster dissociation, 'hit and run' profile; clozapine has high 5HT2:D2 ratio and weak D1/D2 affinity.
Sulpiride: pure D2 antagonist; low doses presynaptic (negative symptoms?), above 800 mg/day postsynaptic (positive symptoms). Amisulpride: D2 and D3 antagonist.
Risperidone at higher doses binds D2 like typicals, giving EPSEs and prolactin effects.
Thioridazine, pericyazine, pipotiazine: marked antimuscarinic effect, fewer EPSEs than other typicals; chlorpromazine and promazine are highly sedative.
Zotepine: potent noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor and antihistaminic; ziprasidone agonistic at 5HT1A with some SNRI action.
Therapeutic effect = mesolimbic D2 blockade; mesocortical = negative symptoms, nigrostriatal = EPSEs, tuberoinfundibular = prolactin.
Clozapine dissociates fastest from the D2 receptor (fast dissociation predicts atypicality).

sections.title: 4. Modes of therapeutic action for psychotropics: antidepressant drugs and lithium

blocks.title: Antidepressant mechanisms by drug
rows: Enhances norepinephrine and dopamine neurotransmission through 5HT2C antagonism (a norepinephrine and dopamine disinhibitor, **NDDI**); also a direct agonist at **melatonin** **MT1** and **MT2** receptors; antidepressant with possible sedative effects

Tetracyclic (dibenzoxazepine); dopamine antagonism plus serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibition, so claimed to have antipsychotic properties; extrapyramidal side effects more often than other tricyclics
Dopamine and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor; used for smoking cessation and depression; no antimuscarinic activity; some competitive nicotinic antagonism
Partial agonist at 5HT1A; presynaptically mostly a full agonist inhibiting serotonin release (antianxiety effect); postsynaptic partial agonism appears to account for antidepressant activity
**SSRI**, most selective of all SSRIs for serotonin reuptake; racemic mixture of which the s isomer is active but the r enantiomer inhibits it, so a lesser dose of **escitalopram** (s) is sufficient
Tricyclic regarded as most potent; higher **SRI** selectivity than other TCAs but lesser than SSRIs
Tricyclic with least anticholinergic action but lethal on overdose
**SNRI** similar to **venlafaxine**; said to have a better profile for psychosomatic and neuropathic pain
Levothyroxine is **T4**, liothyronine is **T3**; thyroid hormones that suppress **TSH** and act as adjuvant in resistant depression; exact antidepressant mechanism unknown, possibly neuroendocrine
5HT2A antagonism, alpha 2 antagonism, antihistaminic and anti-5HT3 properties; **mianserin** has a similar profile but is not antihistaminic and has anticholinergic properties instead
5HT2 antagonist with some serotonin and mild norepinephrine reuptake inhibition; some alpha 1 antagonism; produces mCPP as a metabolite
**SSRI**, most potent in serotonin reuptake blockade but not specific; significant antimuscarinic action
**MAOI**; increased availability of monoamines including serotonin and noradrenaline may explain antidepressant action, though disputed
Beta blocker with intrinsic sympathomimetic activity; also 5HT1A antagonism, tipped to enhance the onset of action of SSRIs
**MAOI** selective for B at normal therapeutic doses; selectivity lost when a patch is applied at higher doses, giving some antidepressant action
Reuptake inhibition at somatodendritic areas soon after administration down-regulates somatic autoreceptors for serotonin, so inhibitory tone is lost and serotonergic output is facilitated
**MAOI**; irreversible, non-selective; positive enantiomer is the better **MAOI**, negative enantiomer the better reuptake inhibitor
5HT2A/2C antagonism and some alpha 2 blockade; alpha 1 blockade and antihistaminic properties; feeble reuptake inhibition at serotonin transporters

Monoamine reuptake inhibition with varying degrees of noradrenaline and serotonin reuptake inhibition; negligible effect on dopamine; **clomipramine** is the most serotonin specific; secondary amines are more noradrenergic
**SNRI**; acts as an **SSRI** at lower (<150 mg) doses
Mechanism not fully understood: selective serotonin reuptake inhibition plus partial agonist action at 5HT1A (structure close to **trazodone** and **nefazodone**)
Structure similar to **reboxetine** but predominantly **SSRI**-like; also 5HT3 antagonism and 5HT1A agonism

blocks.forTopic: MAO inhibitors in the notes' table

blocks.text: **Lithium** is thought to act via the second messenger system. It putatively enhances serotonin transmission by (1) increasing tryptophan uptake into neurons, (2) enhancing serotonin release and (3) downregulation of 5HT1A, 1B and 2 receptor subtypes on chronic administration.

**Lithium** also (4) directly inhibits glycogen synthase kinase-3 (**GSK-3**) and (5) competes with magnesium directly at regulatory enzymes such as inositol-monophosphatase (IMPase), which catalyses the inositol second messenger system.

Inositol depletion hypothesis: inhibition of IMPase by **lithium** reduces myoinositol and phosphoinositide phosphate (**PIP-2**), leading to therapeutic efficacy. Through an increase in intracellular sodium it may also affect the Na+K+ pump and reduce dopamine synthesis in a dose-dependent fashion.

blocks.title: Mechanism of TCA action vs SSRI action (step order as given in the notes' flow diagrams)
rows: Inhibition of nerve terminal **NE** neuronal uptake system
Desensitization of inhibitory alpha2-adrenoceptors in the terminal
Desensitisation of inhibitory 5HT1A autoreceptors in the soma
Further increase in synaptic concentrations of **NE**
Desensitization of postsynaptic beta adrenoceptors without affecting postsynaptic alpha1 sensitivity

blocks.text: Chronic (2-4 weeks) antidepressant/tricyclic treatment **DOWN**-regulates beta-adrenergic receptors (not alpha, not up-regulation); this is **NOT** seen after acute or single doses. The explanation ties beta-receptor down-regulation to the delayed therapeutic effect (still to be clarified) and, in chronic tricyclic users, to hypotensive effects.

**Trazodone** is a **SARI** (potent 5HT2A, dose-dependent 5HT2C and serotonin transporter blockade) that acts like two drugs depending on dose: low-dose hypnotic, higher doses add serotonin reuptake inhibition. 'Mixed serotonin antagonist/agonist' is the keyed receptor profile; its active metabolite mCPP is a 5-**HT2C** agonist.

Norepinephrine reuptake blockade is the property that is **NOT** significant for **trazodone** (serotonin reuptake blockade, antihistamine action, strong alpha-1 antagonism and 5-**HT2** antagonism all are); the explanation notes it is **nefazodone** that also inhibits norepinephrine reuptake.
Priapism with **trazodone** is attributed to alpha-1 **ANTAGONISM** (not alpha-2 or beta-1 effects); the explanation says alpha-1 blockade causes priapism with **trazodone** or **risperidone**.

**Mirtazapine** sedation at a low dose (7.5 mg) is via histamine **H1** blockade, because at low plasma concentrations it has higher affinity for histamine than serotonergic receptors; at higher doses increased noradrenergic transmission offsets the antihistamine effect and reduces sedation.

**Moclobemide** has very limited potential for hypertensive crisis (the keyed answer, against **phenelzine**, **isocarboxazid**, **tranylcypromine** and cocaine): tyramine interactions are rare and mild, though possible with high doses (above 600 mg/day) or large tyramine intake.

**SSRI** 5-**HT2A** stimulation is blamed for sleep disturbance (insomnia), whereas 5-**HT2C** stimulation (5-**HT2A**/2C in the explanation) is blamed for delayed ejaculation and anorgasmia with **fluoxetine**; 5-**HT1A**, 5-**HT3**, **H1**, **D2** and alpha-1 are the distractors.

**Amitriptyline** has less serotonergic effect than the other options and is therefore the **TCA** chosen as comparatively safe with an **MAOI**; the explanation names **clomipramine** as the **TCA** most likely to cause the serious **MAOI-TCA** interaction (excessive serotonin elevation).

blocks.note: Not in the notes. **Q1** (answer dothiepin): **amitriptyline** and dothiepin are more sedative TCAs; **clomipramine**, **imipramine**, **nortriptyline** and **lofepramine** are less sedative.

The notes say only that desipramine has least anticholinergic action but is lethal in overdose. **Q23** (answer desipramine): it has a stimulant effect and is the **TCA** with most evidence for use in **ADHD**.

Not in the notes. **Q16** (answer **amitriptyline**): comparatively safe adjunct to MAOIs per the question; **Q39** (answer add **mirtazapine**): the alpha-2 antagonist **mirtazapine** is often combined with SNRIs such as **venlafaxine** ('California rocket fuel').

Not in the notes. **Q48** (answer **citalopram**): **citalopram** and **escitalopram** are very weak inhibitors of **CYP** 1A2 and 2D6, while **fluoxetine**, **fluvoxamine** and **paroxetine** are potent inhibitors of several hepatic cytochrome enzymes.

items.text: **Reboxetine** is the noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor (blocks the norepinephrine transporter) among **risperidone**, **agomelatine**, **fluoxetine** and **paroxetine**.
**Buspirone** acts on the 5HT1A receptor (partial agonist, pre- and postsynaptic); 5HT2A, **GABA-A** and **GABA-B** are distractors.
Premature ejaculation responds to **fluoxetine** (and **sertraline**): the anorgasmic effects of SSRIs are the reason.
**Fluoxetine**'s anorgasmia is keyed to 5HT-2C stimulation (not alpha-1, **D2**, mu-opioid or 5HT-1A); 5-**HT2A**/2C stimulation by SSRIs can cause delayed ejaculation and anorgasmia.

**Bupropion** is the atypical antidepressant with dopaminergic **AND** noradrenergic actions (not **mirtazapine**, **venlafaxine**, **reboxetine** or **mianserin**); also advocated by **NICE** for smoking cessation.
**Mirtazapine** is the presynaptic alpha-2 antagonist classified as a NaSSA (not **bupropion**, **venlafaxine**, **reboxetine** or **buspirone**).
**Agomelatine** modulates the **melatonin** system directly (**MT1** and **MT2** agonist, 5HT2C antagonist); **trazodone**, **zopiclone**, **perphenazine** and **galantamine** are distractors.
Severely depressed 85-year-old not responding to maximum-dose **venlafaxine**: add **mirtazapine** (the **SNRI** plus alpha-2 antagonist combination, 'California rocket fuel').

blocks.note: Not in the notes. Mock stem (keyed increased expression of corticosteroid receptors in brain): antidepressants reduce **HPA** axis activity by increasing negative feedback from steroid hormone, made possible by increased corticosteroid receptors; increased **CRH**, cortisol, **ACTH** or **HPA** activity are the wrong options.

bullets.text: Reboxetine = NARI; moclobemide = reversible MAO-A inhibitor; tranylcypromine = irreversible non-selective MAOI; selegiline = MAO-B selective at normal doses.
Citalopram most selective SSRI (s isomer active, so escitalopram needs lower dose).
Paroxetine is the most potent SSRI at serotonin reuptake blockade but not specific, with significant antimuscarinic action.
Agomelatine: 5HT2C antagonist (NDDI) plus MT1/MT2 melatonin agonist.
Mirtazapine: 5HT2A antagonism, alpha 2 antagonism, antihistaminic and anti-5HT3 properties.
Lithium: second messenger action; increases tryptophan uptake and serotonin release, down-regulates 5HT1A/1B/2, inhibits GSK-3 and IMPase (inositol depletion hypothesis).
Chronic TCA effect: desensitization of postsynaptic beta adrenoceptors without altering alpha1; SSRI: desensitization of somatodendritic 5HT1A autoreceptors and presynaptic 5HT1B.
Venlafaxine acts as an SSRI below 150 mg; clomipramine is the most serotonin-specific TCA; TCAs have negligible dopamine effect.
Chronic antidepressant/TCA treatment down-regulates beta-adrenergic receptors (not acute).
Mirtazapine sedates at a low dose (7.5 mg) via H1 receptors.

sections.title: 5. Modes of therapeutic action for psychotropics: mood stabilisers

blocks.title: Mood stabiliser and anticonvulsant mechanisms by drug
rows: Prolongs sodium channel inactivation (and so calcium channel inactivation); reduces glutamate neurotransmission; adenosine **A1** antagonism; increases brain catecholamine activity; inhibits peripheral benzodiazepine receptors; reduces limbic kindling; interferes with glial cell steroidogenesis

**GABA** analogue structurally; binds the alpha2delta subunit of the voltage-dependent calcium channel; acts on l-amino acid transport and can increase **GABA** availability; crosses **BBB** via l-**AA** transport; high-affinity site in **GABA-A** complex but no benzodiazepine-like actions
Blocks voltage-sensitive sodium channels, modulating glutamate and aspartate release; some effect on calcium channels; some inhibition of serotonin reuptake and weak inhibition of 5HT3
Indirectly enhances the **GABA** system; anticonvulsant with weak evidence against mania
A metabolite of **carbamazepine**; similar mechanisms proposed

**GABA** analogue (similar to **gabapentin**); binds alpha2delta subunit of the voltage-dependent calcium channel; may influence GABAergic neurotransmission; anti-epileptic, analgesic (neuropathic pain) and anxiolytic effects; more potent than **gabapentin**, hence higher therapeutic index and fewer dose-related side effects
Potent and selective reuptake inhibitor of **GABA**; mild antihistaminic effects

sections.title: 6. Modes of therapeutic action for psychotropics: sedatives and hypnotics

blocks.title: Sedative and hypnotic mechanisms by drug
rows: Act at the omega site on the **GABA-A** complex; all agonists except **clonazepam** (partial agonist); facilitate **GABA** action (inhibition via chloride ions); no direct agonist action without **GABA**; increase the frequency and duration of chloride channel opening, not the number
Barbiturate-like agents, probably potentiate GABAergic neurotransmission; paraldehyde is a cyclic ether; poor safety profile, none in clinical use

**Melatonin** receptor full agonist, high affinity and selectivity for **MT1** and **MT2** over **MT3**; decreases sleep latency, increases sleep time; flat dose-response curve (no difference between 16 mg and 64 mg); may have lower abuse potential than other hypnotics

Act directly on **GABA-A**, opening chloride channels and enhancing hyperpolarisation; at lower doses decrease the rate of **GABA** dissociation and increase the duration (not number) of **GABA**-activated chloride channel opening; at slightly higher concentrations directly open chloride channels even without **GABA**, which benzodiazepines do not

Act via **GABA-A** but differently from benzodiazepines: benzodiazepines occupy all 3 subunits of the omega receptor, Z-drugs only certain subunits; **zolpidem** and **zopiclone** act on omega1 receptors, so no muscle relaxant, anxiolytic or anticonvulsant effects and slow wave sleep unaffected; zaleplon occupies all 3 omega receptors; **zopiclone** is a racemic mixture with only the s-isomer active (eszopiclone)

blocks.text: Given their selectivity on **BDZ**-receptor subunits, Z-drugs are less likely to affect sleep stages and have a lower risk of tolerance and dependence than benzodiazepine hypnotics. **Zopiclone** is the least selective of all Z-drugs.

blocks.title: Benzodiazepines vs barbiturates at the GABA-A chloride channel
rows: Increase frequency and duration of chloride channel opening; not the number of channels
Increase duration (not number) of **GABA**-activated chloride channel opening at lower doses
No direct agonistic action in the absence of **GABA**
At slightly higher concentrations directly activate chloride channel opening even without **GABA**

blocks.text: Benzodiazepines are described as **ALLOSTERIC** modulators of the **GABA-A** receptor: they bind the gamma sub-unit and increase the **FREQUENCY** of channel opening (chloride conductance), and do **NOT** substitute for **GABA**, which binds the alpha sub-unit. 'Reduce **GABA** transmission', 'block sodium reuptake' and 'substitute for **GABA**' are the distractors; contrast barbiturates (duration of opening).

Benzodiazepine activity depends on the **GABA-A** receptor complex (not **GABA-B**, 5HT1A or beta adrenergic complexes); the explanation says **GABA-A** receptors divide into benzodiazepine-sensitive and benzodiazepine-insensitive subtypes depending on subunits.

**Q38** asks the mechanism of barbiturates: the answer is increasing the duration of chloride channel opening. Distractors are increasing the frequency of opening (in the notes, a benzodiazepine action alongside lengthened opening) and increasing the number of channels (neither drug does this).

Withdrawal/discontinuation reactions are more likely with a drug having potent **ANTICHOLINERGIC** properties; slow withdrawal, taking the drug after food and a partial rather than full agonist are the tempting but wrong options.

**Alprazolam** acts on **GABA** (benzodiazepine receptors modulating **GABA** activity), not **NMDA**, **D1**, histaminergic or **M1** receptors; onset and peak levels are quickest for **diazepam**, **lorazepam**, **alprazolam**, triazolam and estazolam.

Partial opioid agonist; mild agonism at lower doses, antagonistic effects at higher doses

sections.title: 8. Modes of therapeutic action for psychotropics: anti-dementia drugs

blocks.title: Anti-dementia drug mechanisms
rows: Cholinesterase inhibitors: inhibit acetylcholinesterase, which breaks down acetylcholine centrally. **Rivastigmine** inhibits both acetyl- and butyrylcholinesterase; **donepezil** and **galantamine** are acetyl specific. **Galantamine** also has nicotinic agonistic properties

Blocks **NMDA** glutamate receptors; unlike **ketamine** (high-affinity noncompetitive blocker) it is a low-affinity non-competitive blocker binding only to actively open **NMDA** channels; fast dissociation, so it does not accumulate or interfere with normal **NMDA** activity

blocks.title: Cholinesterase inhibitor details
rows: By both acetylcholinesterase (AChE) and butyrylcholinesterase (BChE); cholinesterase inhibitors raise ACh by inhibiting these enzymes
Ionic subsite: tacrine and **donepezil**. Catalytic esteratic subsite: physostigmine and **rivastigmine**
Tacrine, and to some extent **rivastigmine**, are non-selective inhibitors of AChE and BChE; **CNS**-specific AChE inhibition can occur with **donepezil**
Reversible or irreversible, competitive or noncompetitive with ACh; **galantamine** competitive, tacrine non-competitive

Tetramer **G4** on presynaptic membranes (decreased with neuronal loss in **AD**); monomer **G1** on postsynaptic membranes (not significantly decreased in **AD** or aging). **Rivastigmine** and to some extent **galantamine** are highly selective for **G1**; **donepezil** is not selective

blocks.text: **Galantamine** is the anti-dementia drug acting directly on nicotinic receptors (agonist at nicotinic sites, unlike other cholinesterase inhibitors; also a reversible, competitive AChE inhibitor); **donepezil**, tacrine, **rivastigmine** and **memantine** are the distractors.

**Galantamine** is the agent with an **ALLOSTERIC** action on nicotinic receptors (binding a site different from the ACh binding site, amplifying ACh action and circumventing tolerance); the explanation notes that AChE inhibitors give only short-term symptomatic improvement, and that long-term nicotinic agonists desensitise receptors.

blocks.title: Riluzole
rows: Approved for Motor Neuron Disorder; unclear whether it helps fronto-temporal dementia features associated with **MND**; prolongs survival by nearly ==10%== for more than a year of treatment
Sodium channel blockade; high-voltage calcium channel blockade; **NMDA**-glutamate receptor antagonism
Preferentially blocks sodium channels in damaged neurons, reducing calcium flow and indirectly preventing excitotoxic damage

blocks.text: **Memantine** is a **NON-COMPETITIVE** **NMDA** receptor antagonist (not an agonist, competitive blocker or AChE inhibitor); unlike **ketamine** (a high-affinity noncompetitive blocker), it has low affinity and fast dissociation, binds only actively open **NMDA** channels and so does not interfere with normal **NMDA** activity.

Excitotoxicity from glutamatergic overstimulation is the rationale for **memantine** (not selegiline, **donepezil**, **risperidone** or **galantamine**): a non-competitive **NMDA** antagonist that may be neuroprotective, licensed for moderate to severe Alzheimer dementia.
Riluzole's efficacy in motor neuron disease is explained by **NMDA** receptor blockade (not AChE, **AMPA**, **GABA** or **D5** effects): riluzole is an **NMDA** antagonist similar to **memantine**.

blocks.note: Not in the notes. **Q50** (answer: reverses progression of neuropathological degeneration has no support): **donepezil** may improve symptoms and slow progression but does not reverse the degenerative process; it can delay behavioural problems and nursing home placement, preserve activities of daily living and reduce caregiver burden.

blocks.text: For **donepezil** the statement with **NO** evidence-based support is that it reverses the progression of neuropathological degeneration; reduced caregiver burden, improved activities of daily living and neuropsychiatric symptoms and delayed institutionalisation **ARE** supported.

rows: Serotonin 2C receptor agonist; given twice daily and discontinued if ==5%== weight loss is not achieved by 12 weeks; commonest side effect headache; can induce hypoglycaemia in diabetic patients

blocks.text: **Atomoxetine**'s mechanism in **ADHD** is selective noradrenaline reuptake inhibition (**NARI**, like **reboxetine**), not dopaminergic agonism, glutamatergic antagonism, serotonin reuptake or dopamine reuptake inhibition.

Amantadine is the drug with dual action: antiviral (prevents viral uncoating, influenza prophylaxis) and in Parkinsonism (induces dopamine release from nerve terminals); carbidopa, **levodopa**, orphenadrine and bromocriptine are the distractors.

Cyproheptadine blocks histamine **H1** receptors (and is also a 5-**HT2** antagonist, not a 5HT3 blocker or **H2** blocker); it has been used for **SSRI**-induced sexual dysfunction, particularly anorgasmia, with some evidence in antipsychotic akathisia.

**Risperidone** akathisia plus depressive symptoms: **mirtazapine** is keyed (not **venlafaxine**, **amitriptyline**, **paroxetine** or **fluoxetine**); the explanation lists other helpful drugs as **propranolol** (30-80 mg/day), low-dose **clonazepam** and 5-**HT2** antagonists (cyproheptadine, **mianserin**, **trazodone**, diphenhydramine).

blocks.text: Repeated subconvulsive electrical stimulation in animals reduces seizure threshold (kindling). **ECT** does not produce a kindling effect and protects against kindling in animal studies, so it can be termed an anti-kindling agent; dosing may need to increase over the course of treatment to achieve the same seizure-inducing effect.
Hippocampal neuronal loss occurs in kindling, but **ECT** results in neurogenesis in the rat, possibly via increased expression of brain-derived neurotrophic factor and its receptor.
Blood-brain barrier permeability increases acutely after **ECT** but returns to baseline within 24 hours.

Imaging studies show **ECT** is not associated with markers of cell loss or damage: no change in myelin basic protein immunoreactivity or serum neuron-specific enolase; tau, neurofilament and S-100 beta (markers of neuronal and glial damage) are also unchanged.
**EEG** shows delta and theta activity after **ECT**; this pattern returns to normal 3 months after the end of treatment.

blocks.text: Ethnicity is a self-ascribed belongingness to a group with common geographical origins, race, language, religion etc.; ethnic categories retain a strong racial component. Race is largely perceived by appearance and attributed to biological and genetic traits. Culture is a shared system of concepts or mental representations established by convention and transmitted traditionally.
Differences exist in placebo response, compliance, doctor-patient relationship, social stress and health beliefs, in addition to differences in the pharmacology of drugs.

Absorption: Caucasians appear to have lower plasma levels of tricyclics and attain peaks later than Asians, attributed to a greater incidence of slow hydroxylation among Asians. Maximal plasma **haloperidol** after rapid tranquillisation is significantly higher in Asians than Caucasians.

**CYP2D6** variation is largely genetically determined (it metabolises many antidepressants, antipsychotics, beta-blockers and antiarrhythmics) and is called debrisoquine/sparteine polymorphism, with 4 groups.

blocks.title: CYP2D6 metabolizer groups
rows: Develop side effects quickly; lack the enzyme, so poor metabolizers of **risperidone** and tricyclics. Caucasians highest (nearly ==7%==), East Asians lowest (==1%==)
Higher in Asians (most Asians fall here, hence more side effects though good efficacy)
Listed as a group; no detail given on that page

Need high doses; ==33%== of North Africans have multiple copies of **CYP2D6** and need higher **risperidone** doses; only ==5%== of Caucasians and ==1%== of East Asians; ==25%== of Indians may have this variant

blocks.text: **CYP2C19** metabolises omeprazole, **propranolol** and psychotropics such as hexobarbital, **diazepam**, **citalopram**, **imipramine**, **clomipramine**, **sertraline** and **amitriptyline**.
Poor metabolizers of **CYP2C19** substrates are much more frequent in Asians (15-==30%==) than in Caucasians (3-==6%==); the polymorphism is mephenytoin related.
Unlike **CYP2D6**, variations in **CYP3A4** are often influenced by environmental (e.g. diet) factors.
Nearly ==40%== of Asians and around ==60%== of South American Native Indians lack sufficient aldehyde dehydrogenase to metabolise alcohol, a natural deterrent in these communities.

Pharmacodynamics: the long form serotonin transporter polymorphism in Caucasians is associated with better **SSRI** response and tolerance, the opposite being true in South East Asians. Low **COMT** variant is seen in under ==20%== of Asians and Africans but nearly ==50%== of Caucasians.

Adverse effects: East Asians are most likely to be rapid acetylators of isoniazid and suffer hepatotoxicity, with less peripheral neuropathy (seen in slow acetylators). Chinese people had higher extrapyramidal side effects with **haloperidol** and comparably high blood levels at equivalent doses.

Asian subjects produced greater serum prolactin than Caucasians on antipsychotics, still significant after controlling for **haloperidol** concentration, suggesting a difference in dopamine receptor-mediated response.

bullets.text: CYP2D6 groups: poor, intermediate, extensive, ultrarapid; poor metabolizers highest in Caucasians (nearly 7%), lowest in East Asians (1%).
Most Asians are intermediate CYP2D6 metabolizers (more side effects, good efficacy); 33% of North Africans are ultrarapid and need higher risperidone doses.
CYP2C19 poor metabolizers: Asians 15-30% vs Caucasians 3-6%; CYP3A4 variation is environmentally influenced.
About 40% of Asians and 60% of South American Native Indians lack enough aldehyde dehydrogenase to metabolise alcohol.
Long form 5-HTT polymorphism: better SSRI response in Caucasians, opposite in South East Asians; low COMT variant under 20% Asians/Africans, nearly 50% Caucasians.
Asians: start at half the standard dose; slow TCA metabolism; higher prolactin on antipsychotics; Chinese more EPSE on haloperidol.
African Americans: more lithium/TCA side effects, higher TD, poor fluoxetine response.

blocks.text: Antipsychotic response is shown to be superior in women. In chronically ill populations men require twice as high a dose as women for effective maintenance, and women have higher antipsychotic plasma levels than men at the same dose.

**CYP1A2** appears less active in women than men, giving relatively higher blood concentrations of **olanzapine** and **clozapine** in women. The volume of distribution of lipophilic drugs such as antipsychotics is greater in women.

In women blood volume is smaller but lipid compartments larger, which prolongs antipsychotic half-life and leads to accumulation over time, important with depot injections; after steady state, dosing intervals for women should be longer than for men.

Acute dystonia, long thought commoner in men, is now shown to be more frequent in females at equivalent doses (earlier studies did not account for young men commonly receiving higher doses). Pulmonary embolism (rare, with drugs having affinity for 5-**HT2A**) and tardive dyskinesia appear more common in women.
